lessons.title: The Healing Cut: Launching Our Investigation Into Why Cells Look Different

quiz.prompt: Amina cuts her finger while slicing onions in the kitchen in Eastleigh. She presses the cut with her thumb. After about a minute, what does she notice?
choices: The bleeding is slowing and a dark, sticky material is starting to form
A scab has formed and is beginning to fall off
The cut has closed and there is no sign of any injury
The bleeding has completely stopped and new pink skin has already grown
quiz.rationale: In the narrated scenario, after about a minute the bleeding slows and a dark, sticky material begins to form. The scab and new skin only appear over the following days.
quiz.placement: Predict: teacher narrates Amina's cut and learners write in their science notebooks

quiz.prompt: A four-image sequence shows Amina's cut finger healing. Which order shows what learners observed, from first to last?
choices: Scab on healing skin, fresh cut with blood, new pink skin, dark clot forming
Fresh cut with blood, dark clot forming, scab on healing skin after two days, new pink skin with the scab gone
Fresh cut with blood, new pink skin, dark clot forming, scab on healing skin
Dark clot forming, fresh cut with blood, new pink skin, scab on healing skin
quiz.rationale: The sequence runs: (1) fresh cut with blood, (2) dark clot forming, (3) scab after two days, (4) new pink skin with the scab gone.
quiz.placement: Observe: four-image photo sequence of the healing finger and Think-Pair-Share

quiz.prompt: A learner says, "The blood goes hard, white cells come, and skin grows back." Which statement best describes what the healing finger shows about the body's response to injury?
choices: Each job happens one at a time, and the next job cannot start until the first has finished completely
Only one single process happens, and it does every job in the wound
The body only stops the bleeding and does nothing else until the skin is healed
The body does several different things at the same time, such as stopping bleeding, fighting germs and rebuilding skin
quiz.rationale: The lesson shows that healing is not one process but many going on together, such as stopping bleeding, fighting infection and rebuilding skin. Learners begin to see that different responses may involve different types of cells.
quiz.placement: Explain: whole-class discussion on 'one thing or many things' doing the healing job

quiz.prompt: At the end of the discussion, the teacher says that dozens of different tiny structures work together in a healing wound, and that each looks different from the others. A learner asks, "So why do they all look so different from each other?" What is the best response at this point in the unit?
choices: They look different because each one eats different food
They look different because each one has different DNA from the others
This question has not been answered yet; it is the big question we will investigate in the coming lessons
They look different because each one is a different age
quiz.rationale: This is the launch lesson and the phenomenon is deliberately left unexplained. The 'why' is the question the class will investigate across the unit, so learners should not settle on a ready-made answer.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher's bridging statement and 'Does that surprise you? Why?' follow-up

quiz.prompt: On the Driving Question Board, learners write one 'What do we notice?' note and one 'What do we wonder?' note. Which of these is a good 'What do we wonder?' note?
choices: The finger looks almost the same as before after a few days
How does the body know exactly what shape of skin to rebuild?
A dark clot formed on the cut
The bleeding slowed down after about a minute
quiz.rationale: A 'wonder' note is a genuine question. The other three are statements of things that can be seen, so they belong in the 'notice' column.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: yellow 'What do we notice?' and blue 'What do we wonder?' sticky notes

quiz.prompt: Which question is the driving question introduced from the top of the Driving Question Board for this unit on cells?
choices: How do plants make their own food using sunlight?
How many cells are there in a human finger?
Why does the human body feel pain when it is cut?
Why do cells in our body look so different from each other, and how does the shape of a cell determine the job it can do?
quiz.rationale: The driving question links the puzzle of the healing cut to cell shape and job. It will be answered piece by piece across the unit.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: teacher reads the driving question aloud from the top of the poster

quiz.prompt: In Version 0 of the cell model, learners draw what they think a cell looks like, without any diagrams or notes. Why do they draw it this way?
choices: To record what they think now, so they can compare it with their final model in Lesson 12
To copy the correct cell diagram so that they remember it for the exam
To test who can draw the most accurate cell in the class
To mark the drawings as right or wrong before the unit begins
quiz.rationale: Version 0 is a baseline of learners' current ideas. It is not a test, and it will be compared with the final model at the end of the unit to show how their thinking has changed.
quiz.placement: Model: Version 0 'Draw what you think a cell looks like'

lessons.title: What Is a Cell? Introduction to Cell Theory

quiz.prompt: In the ugali kitchen analogy, the kitchen door is compared to the cell membrane. Which statement shows where this analogy does NOT match a real cell?
choices: A kitchen door is found at the edge of the kitchen, but the cell membrane is found at the edge of the cell.
A kitchen door lets anything through when it is open, but the cell membrane chooses what passes in and out all the time.
A kitchen door can be opened and closed, but the cell membrane can also let some things pass.
A kitchen door separates the inside from the outside, but the cell membrane does not separate anything.
quiz.rationale: A kitchen door is open or shut and lets anything through when open, while the cell membrane is selective all the time. This is one of the places where the analogy breaks down.
quiz.placement: Part A: The Ugali Kitchen Analogy

quiz.prompt: Which feature belongs to a prokaryotic cell such as E. coli (a bacterium)?
choices: It has a nucleus surrounded by a membrane.
It has mitochondria.
Its DNA floats freely in the cell and is not inside a membrane-bound nucleus.
It is found only in plants.
quiz.rationale: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound nucleus, so their DNA floats freely in the cell. Mitochondria and a membrane-bound nucleus are features of eukaryotic cells.
quiz.placement: Part C: Prokaryote vs. Eukaryote Sort

quiz.prompt: Which of these is one of the three tenets (main ideas) of cell theory?
choices: All living things are made of one or more cells.
All cells in one organism look the same.
New cells can form from non-living matter.
Every cell has a nucleus.
quiz.rationale: Cell theory states that all living things are made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and that all cells come from pre-existing cells. Bacteria have no nucleus, and cells arise only from other cells.
quiz.placement: Part B: Guided Research & Diagram Study (Cell Theory Evidence Table)

quiz.prompt: A student says, "Ribosomes are found only in eukaryotic cells, so bacteria cannot make proteins." Which response is correct?
choices: The student is wrong because ribosomes are found only in plant cells and bacteria.
The student is correct because ribosomes are found only in animal cells.
The student is correct because bacteria have no organelles at all.
The student is wrong because ribosomes are present in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, so bacteria can make proteins.
quiz.rationale: Ribosomes are present in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, so even the simplest bacteria can make proteins. This was the most commonly misplaced card in the sort.
quiz.placement: Explain: mini-lecture correcting card-sort errors and colour-coding the ARES diagram cards

quiz.prompt: A learner cuts a finger and new skin grows in from the edges of the cut over a few days. Which explanation uses cell theory correctly?
choices: The new skin cells came from existing skin cells at the edge of the cut, because all cells come from pre-existing cells.
The new skin cells appeared from non-living material in the scab, because cells can form on their own.
The new skin cells came from platelets, because platelets are the basic unit of all skin.
The new skin cells formed from the blood clot, because the clot turns into skin.
quiz.rationale: Virchow's tenet says all cells come from pre-existing cells. So new skin cells must have been made when existing skin cells divided.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER paragraph on how Amina's body produced new skin cells

quiz.prompt: Otieno draws a model of an animal cell for his Version 1 notebook page and labels a cell wall on it. What should his teacher tell him?
choices: Remove it, because no cells have a cell wall.
Keep it, because only animal cells have a cell wall.
Remove it, because animal cells do not have a cell wall, although plant cells and bacteria do.
Keep it, because all cells have a cell wall.
quiz.rationale: Animal cells lack a cell wall. Plant cells (cellulose) and bacteria (peptidoglycan) have one, so the idea that only plants have cell walls is also a misconception.
quiz.placement: Model: Version 1 of the Cumulative Cell Model (sketch and labels)

quiz.prompt: Bacteria have no nucleus, yet they are still cells. Which of these do ALL cells, including bacteria, have?
choices: Mitochondria
DNA (genetic material) inside a cell membrane
A nucleus with a membrane around it
Chloroplasts
quiz.rationale: Every cell has a cell membrane and DNA. A membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts are not found in all cells, because prokaryotes lack them.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: answering 'What do ALL cells have in common?'

lessons.title: Prokaryotic vs. Eukaryotic Cells: Two Worlds Inside One Body

quiz.prompt: E. coli is a prokaryote that can cause food poisoning in poorly stored nyama choma. Which statement correctly describes where its genetic material (DNA) is found?
choices: E. coli has no DNA at all because it has no nucleus
The circular DNA lies in a nucleoid region in the cytoplasm, with no nuclear membrane around it
The DNA is enclosed in a nucleus with a nuclear membrane, just like in a human cheek cell
The DNA is kept inside mitochondria
quiz.rationale: A prokaryote has its circular DNA in the nucleoid region, which is not surrounded by a nuclear membrane. It still has DNA, but not a membrane-bound nucleus.
quiz.placement: Comparison table: genetic material location and presence of a membrane-bound nucleus (E. coli vs human cheek cell)

quiz.prompt: A learner says: "E. coli and a human cheek cell both have ribosomes, so they must be the same type of cell." Which response is correct?
choices: Ribosomes are present only in E. coli, because they are needed by prokaryotes
Ribosomes are present in both cells and are not membrane-bound, so having ribosomes does not make the cells the same type
Ribosomes are present only in the cheek cell, because they are membrane-bound organelles
Ribosomes are absent from both cells, because both are too small to have them
quiz.rationale: Ribosomes are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes and are not surrounded by a membrane. The difference lies in membrane-bound organelles, which only eukaryotes have.
quiz.placement: Whole-class review of the comparison table: the ribosome row and membrane-bound organelles

quiz.prompt: A human cheek cell is about 25 times bigger than an E. coli cell. If E. coli is about 2 micrometres long, about how big is the cheek cell?
choices: 50 micrometres
500 micrometres
12.5 micrometres
27 micrometres
quiz.rationale: Multiply the size of E. coli by 25: 2 × 25 = 50 micrometres. This fits the 10–100 micrometre range for eukaryotic cells such as the cheek cell.
quiz.placement: Comparison table: approximate size (E. coli 1–5 micrometres, cheek cell 10–100 micrometres)

quiz.prompt: Which statement about cell walls is correct for E. coli and a human cheek cell?
choices: Neither cell has any structure outside the plasma membrane
E. coli has a cell wall made of peptidoglycan, while the human cheek cell has no cell wall
Both have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan
E. coli has no cell wall, while the human cheek cell has a peptidoglycan cell wall
quiz.rationale: E. coli has a peptidoglycan cell wall outside its plasma membrane. A human cheek cell is an animal cell and has only a cell membrane, with no cell wall.
quiz.placement: Comparison table: cell wall (present or absent; composition)

quiz.prompt: Bacteria that could infect a cut on a finger are prokaryotes. Which observation best shows that they are built differently from the body's skin cells?
choices: They have no membrane-bound nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles
They contain DNA, which skin cells do not contain
They are bigger than skin cells
They have ribosomes, which skin cells do not have
quiz.rationale: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, unlike the eukaryotic cells of the body. Ribosomes and DNA are present in both, and bacteria are much smaller, not bigger.
quiz.placement: Cold-call consolidation round: Brian's question applying prokaryote vs eukaryote to Amina's cut

quiz.prompt: The word "eukaryote" comes from the Greek words eu = true and karyon = nucleus. What does the word tell us about a eukaryotic cell?
choices: It has a true nucleus, enclosed by a nuclear membrane
It lives before other cells appeared
It has no nucleus
It is a very small cell with a cell wall
quiz.rationale: Eu means true and karyon means nucleus, so a eukaryote has a true, membrane-bound nucleus. A prokaryote (pro = before) is a cell with no true nucleus.
quiz.placement: Formal introduction of the terms prokaryote and eukaryote with their Greek etymologies

quiz.prompt: A learner draws two cells side by side and uses a colour code: orange = feature found in prokaryotes only, blue = feature found in eukaryotes only, green = feature found in both. What colour should the learner use to annotate ribosomes?
choices: Ribosomes should not be annotated, because they are not found in either cell
Orange, because ribosomes are found in prokaryotes only
Green, because ribosomes are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes
Blue, because ribosomes are found in eukaryotes only
quiz.rationale: Ribosomes are present in both E. coli and the human cheek cell, so they belong in the green (both) category.
quiz.placement: Version 1 add-on: Prokaryote vs. Eukaryote model with the orange/blue/green colour code

lessons.title: Plant Cell Ultrastructure — Every Organelle Has a Farming Job

quiz.prompt: Before the diagram was shown, some learners predicted that animal cells also contain chloroplasts. Which statement is correct about chloroplasts?
choices: Chloroplasts are found only in animal cells because they need extra energy
Chloroplasts are found in plant cells, where they capture sunlight to make food; animal cells such as cheek cells do not have them
Chloroplasts release energy from glucose in both plant and animal cells
Chloroplasts are found in both plant and animal cells because all cells need to make food
quiz.rationale: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis and are found in plant cells, not in animal cells, which get their food by eating. Releasing energy from glucose is the job of mitochondria.
quiz.placement: Predict: blank plant cell outline and the show-of-hands poll on chloroplasts

quiz.prompt: A learner looks at a plant cell through a school light microscope at about ×400. Which structure would they NOT be able to see clearly, and why?
choices: The whole cell, because light microscopes cannot magnify cells
The nucleus, because it is too small to be separated by a light microscope
Ribosomes, because they are too small to be separated by a light microscope
The large central vacuole, because light cannot pass through water
quiz.rationale: A light microscope has limited resolution (about 0.2 micrometres), so it shows cells, the nucleus and the vacuole but not tiny ultrastructure such as ribosomes. An electron microscope is needed for those.
quiz.placement: Observe: Light vs Electron microscope two-row table

quiz.prompt: Which pair correctly describes the difference between magnification and resolution?
choices: Magnification is how close two points can be and still be seen as two; resolution is how many times bigger the image is
Magnification and resolution both mean how clear the colours are in the image
Magnification is the brightness of the image; resolution is the size of the specimen
Magnification is how many times bigger the image is; resolution is how close two points can be and still be seen as two separate points
quiz.rationale: Magnification is enlargement of the image. Resolution is the ability to show two close points as separate, which is why an electron microscope shows more detail.
quiz.placement: Observe: Light vs Electron microscope two-row table

quiz.prompt: In the Rift Valley maize farm metaphor, the 'farm generator' is the organelle that releases energy from glucose. Which organelle is this, and does a plant cell need it?
choices: Golgi apparatus; plant cells need it to release energy from glucose
Mitochondria; plant cells do not need them because chloroplasts already make their energy
Chloroplast; plant cells need it because it releases energy from glucose
Mitochondria; plant cells need them because chloroplasts make glucose but mitochondria release its energy
quiz.rationale: Chloroplasts make glucose using light, while mitochondria release energy from glucose through respiration. Plant cells need both, for example a seedling growing in the dark still needs energy.
quiz.placement: Explain: Maize Farm Metaphor Table, Mitochondria line and misconception check

quiz.prompt: A plant cell has a rigid structure outside its cell membrane that gives the cell shape, support and protection, like the perimeter fence of a farm. What is this structure?
choices: Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Cell wall
Large central vacuole
Golgi apparatus
quiz.rationale: The cell wall lies outside the cell membrane and provides shape, support and protection. The membrane is the 'farm gate' that controls what enters and leaves.
quiz.placement: Explain: Organelle Job Card matching task

quiz.prompt: A cell makes proteins that must be sorted, modified and sent to other parts of the cell, like goods in a packaging and dispatch depot. Which organelle plays this depot role?
choices: Ribosome
Mitochondrion
Golgi apparatus
Nucleus
quiz.rationale: The Golgi apparatus sorts, modifies and ships proteins and lipids. Ribosomes build the proteins and the nucleus holds the DNA instructions.
quiz.placement: Explain: Organelle Job Card matching task

quiz.prompt: The epidermal cells that grew back over a cut finger are animal cells with no chloroplasts. What is the best explanation?
choices: They do not need any energy to rebuild the skin, so they have no organelles
They lost their chloroplasts because the cut damaged them
They have chloroplasts but these are too small to see
They do not photosynthesise because they get energy from food, so chloroplasts would be wasteful: structure matches function
quiz.rationale: Animal cells get energy from food and do not photosynthesise, so they have no chloroplasts. A cell has the organelles its job demands.
quiz.placement: DQB: connecting line about plant cells and Amina's epidermal cells (also the phenomenon reconnect in Explain)

quiz.prompt: When drawing the Version 2 plant cell model, which drawing is correct?
choices: The cell membrane outside the cell wall, with a small vacuole at the edge
No cell wall, a large central vacuole and chloroplasts only in the nucleus
The cell wall outside the cell membrane, a large vacuole in the centre, and chloroplasts as oval structures inside the cell
The cell wall inside the nucleus, with chloroplasts outside the cell
quiz.rationale: In a plant cell the cell wall is outside the membrane, the vacuole is large and central, and chloroplasts are distinct oval structures in the cytoplasm.
quiz.placement: Model: drawing Version 2 – the Plant Cell

quiz.prompt: Which organelle is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells such as the human cheek cell?
choices: Ribosome
Mitochondrion
Nucleus
Chloroplast
quiz.rationale: Chloroplasts (like the cell wall and large central vacuole) are plant features. Nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes are shared with animal cells.
quiz.placement: Model: red/green colour-coding of plant-only and shared organelles

lessons.title: Animal Cell Ultrastructure — Comparing Plant and Animal Cells

quiz.prompt: Which of these organelles is found in BOTH plant cells and animal cells?
choices: Large central vacuole
Cell wall
Chloroplast
Mitochondrion
quiz.rationale: Mitochondria release energy in both plant and animal cells. Chloroplasts, the cell wall and the large central vacuole are found only in plant cells.
quiz.placement: Think-Pair-Share on the blank animal cell outline and the Prediction Wall (confident vs unsure organelles)

quiz.prompt: A group fills in its Comparison Table and writes a tick for 'large central vacuole' in the animal cell column. What is the correct statement?
choices: Animal cells have a large central vacuole but no small ones.
Animal cells have a large central vacuole, just like plant cells.
Animal cells have only small, temporary vacuoles. The large central vacuole belongs to plant cells.
Animal cells have no vacuoles of any kind.
quiz.rationale: Animal cells have small, numerous vacuoles. The large central vacuole stores water and maintains turgor in plant cells, so it should be marked absent in animal cells.
quiz.placement: Three-column Comparison Table (plant vs animal organelles) completed in groups of 4

quiz.prompt: When a Grade 10 student cuts a finger, neutrophils arrive at the wound and engulf bacteria. Which organelle in the neutrophil digests the engulfed bacteria?
choices: Mitochondrion, which releases energy from glucose
Lysosome, a membrane-bound sac of digestive enzymes
Centriole, which organises spindle fibres
Ribosome, which joins amino acids to make proteins
quiz.rationale: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down engulfed bacteria. The other organelles have different jobs: energy release, protein making and cell division.
quiz.placement: Guided explanation: return to the phenomenon, 'What organelle makes that digestion possible?' (lysosomes)

quiz.prompt: Epidermal (skin) cells divide rapidly to close the surface of a cut finger. Which organelle found in animal cells helps organise the spindle fibres during this cell division?
choices: Chloroplast
Centriole
Golgi apparatus
Lysosome
quiz.rationale: Centrioles organise the spindle fibres during animal cell division. Lysosomes digest material, chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, and the Golgi apparatus processes and packages substances.
quiz.placement: Guided explanation: centrioles and epidermal cells dividing to close the wound

quiz.prompt: A neutrophil squeezes through the wall of a capillary to reach a cut on the finger. Why is it important that animal cells have NO cell wall?
choices: Without a cell wall, the cell can make its own food by photosynthesis.
Without a cell wall, the cell does not need a cell membrane.
Without a cell wall, the cell can change shape and move through narrow gaps.
Without a cell wall, the cell can store large amounts of water for support.
quiz.rationale: Animal cells are flexible because they lack a rigid cell wall, so a neutrophil can change shape to pass through the capillary wall. Photosynthesis and water storage are not linked to the absence of a cell wall, and every cell still has a membrane.
quiz.placement: Guided explanation: cell wall, 'Could it do that with a rigid cell wall?'

quiz.prompt: Skin cells in a person's finger have no chloroplasts. What is the best explanation?
choices: Skin cells get energy from glucose carried in the blood, so they do not photosynthesise and do not need chloroplasts.
Skin cells are too small to hold chloroplasts.
Chloroplasts are destroyed when the skin is cut.
Skin cells get their energy directly from sunlight using mitochondria.
quiz.rationale: Animal cells do not make their own food by photosynthesis. They obtain glucose from the bloodstream and release its energy in mitochondria, so chloroplasts would serve no purpose.
quiz.placement: Written 3-sentence Functional Justification: why an animal cell does not need a chloroplast

quiz.prompt: In a Version 3 model, a learner colours the organelles found ONLY in animal cells (not in plant cells) blue. Which pair of organelles should be coloured blue?
choices: Ribosomes and large central vacuole
Nucleus and mitochondria
Lysosomes and centrioles
Chloroplasts and cell wall
quiz.rationale: Lysosomes and centrioles are the organelles unique to animal cells. Chloroplasts, the cell wall and the large central vacuole are plant-only, while the nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes are shared.
quiz.placement: Version 3 side-by-side Plant vs Animal model with colour-coding (blue animal-only, red plant-only, green shared)

lessons.title: Microscopy Practical 1 — Observing Onion Epidermal Cells

quiz.prompt: A Grade 10 learner looks at onion epidermal cells under a compound light microscope at high power (×400). Which of these can the learner see as a clearly separate structure?
choices: The cell membrane as a separate layer inside the cell wall
The cell wall around each cell
Chloroplasts packed in the cytoplasm
Ribosomes inside the cytoplasm
quiz.rationale: The cell wall is thick enough to see as the outer boundary of each cell. The cell membrane is too thin to see separately from the wall with a light microscope, and onion skin has no chloroplasts.
quiz.placement: Part B: group practical, labelling cell wall, vacuole, nucleus and cytoplasm

quiz.prompt: During the teacher demonstration, the coverslip is lowered onto the onion skin at an angle, like closing a book slowly. Why is this done?
choices: To stretch the onion skin so that it becomes thinner
To avoid trapping air bubbles over the tissue
To make the iodine stain spread faster
To kill the cells so they stop moving
quiz.rationale: Lowering the coverslip slowly at an angle pushes air out and so avoids air bubbles, which would spoil the view of the cells.
quiz.placement: Part A: teacher demonstration of slide preparation

quiz.prompt: A learner has just put a prepared onion slide on the microscope stage. Which is the best way to begin focusing?
choices: Remove the coverslip so that the light can reach the cells
Start at low power and use the coarse focus wheel first, then fine focus
Start at high power (×400) because it shows the cells biggest
Use the fine focus only, at any power
quiz.rationale: Low power gives a wider field of view, so the cells are easier to find. Focus with the coarse wheel first, then the fine focus, before moving to a higher power.
quiz.placement: Part A: teacher demonstration, Step 5 (placing the slide and focusing)

quiz.prompt: One drop of iodine solution is added to the onion epidermis on the slide. What is the main reason for adding it?
choices: It makes the cells grow larger so they are easier to see
It adds chloroplasts to the cells
It keeps the onion skin fresh for several days
It makes the nucleus and other structures easier to see
quiz.rationale: Iodine stains parts of the cell, such as the nucleus, so that they show up clearly under the microscope. It does not make cells grow or add structures.
quiz.placement: Part A: teacher demonstration, Step 3 (adding the iodine stain)

quiz.prompt: A learner measures the diameter of the field of view at low power as 4 mm. Along the long side of the cells, 16 onion cells fit across the field. What is the estimated length of one cell?
choices: 0.25 micrometres
25 micrometres
64 mm
250 micrometres
quiz.rationale: Length of one cell = field diameter ÷ number of cells = 4 mm ÷ 16 = 0.25 mm. Since 1 mm = 1000 micrometres, this is 250 micrometres.
quiz.placement: Part B: cell size estimate (field diameter ÷ number of cells)

quiz.prompt: Learners looked at onion epidermal cells under the microscope and found no chloroplasts. Which explanation is best supported by this evidence and by where onions grow?
choices: Onion cells are animal cells, and animal cells never have chloroplasts
The onion bulb grows underground where there is no light, so its cells do not need chloroplasts to capture light
The iodine stain destroyed the chloroplasts
The microscope was not strong enough to show chloroplasts
quiz.rationale: Chloroplasts capture light for photosynthesis. The onion bulb is an underground storage organ that gets no light, so its epidermal cells do not make chloroplasts.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: 'Why are there no chloroplasts in onion epidermal cells?'

quiz.prompt: Leaf cells of a plant have chloroplasts, but onion epidermal cells from the same kind of plant do not. What does this show about cells?
choices: The onion is not really a plant
All plant cells must have the same structures and the same job
Onion cells have lost all their structures
Cells in different parts of one organism can be different because each is specialised for a different job
quiz.rationale: Cells in different parts of the same organism have different structures that suit their jobs. This is cell specialisation: leaf cells carry out photosynthesis, while onion epidermal cells are specialised for protection and storage.
quiz.placement: Whole-class discussion linking the absence of chloroplasts to cell specialisation

quiz.prompt: A learner is updating a plant cell model after looking at onion skin cells. Which annotation about chloroplasts is correct?
choices: Chloroplasts are found only in cells exposed to light, such as leaf cells, and not in onion epidermis or human cells
Chloroplasts are found in every plant cell, including onion epidermis
Chloroplasts are found in all living cells, including human cells
Chloroplasts are found only in cells that grow in the dark
quiz.rationale: Chloroplasts are present in cells exposed to light that photosynthesise, such as leaf cells. They are absent from onion epidermal cells, which grow underground, and from animal cells.
quiz.placement: Revising the Version 3 plant cell model, revision prompt 3 (chloroplast annotation)

lessons.title: Microscopy Practical 2 — Human Cheek Cells: Observing Animal Cell Structure

quiz.prompt: You have drawn and labelled an onion epidermal cell. You are about to look at a cell from the inside of your own cheek. Which structure should you predict you will NOT see in the cheek cell?
choices: Cell membrane
Nucleus
Cell wall
Cytoplasm
quiz.rationale: Cheek cells are animal cells, and animal cells have no rigid cell wall. They do have a nucleus, cell membrane and cytoplasm, as plant cells do.
quiz.placement: Prediction Card: 'I predict I will see ___ and I predict I will NOT see ___'

quiz.prompt: In the cheek cell practical, a drop of methylene blue stain is added to the smear on the slide. Why is the stain used?
choices: It colours parts of the cells, especially the nucleus, so they show up more clearly
It makes the cheek cells grow larger so they are easier to see
It kills bacteria so the cheek cells can be seen more safely
It makes a cell wall form around each cell
quiz.rationale: Cheek cells are almost transparent. Methylene blue stains them, mainly the nucleus, so their structure can be seen and drawn.
quiz.placement: Slide preparation: adding ONE drop of methylene blue stain to the cheek smear

quiz.prompt: A learner views cheek cells using the ×40 objective lens. The eyepiece lens is ×10. What is the total magnification to record on the drawing?
quiz.rationale: Total magnification = objective × eyepiece = 40 × 10 = ×400.
quiz.placement: Focusing the microscope under high power and recording TOTAL magnification on the drawing

quiz.prompt: The cheek cell smear should be spread thinly on the slide. Why?
choices: A thick smear makes the stain wash off
A thick smear makes cells overlap, so individual cells cannot be seen clearly
A thin smear makes the cell wall easier to see
A thin smear makes the cells divide so there are more of them
quiz.rationale: If the smear is too thick, cells pile on top of each other and light cannot pass through. A thin layer lets single cells be seen and drawn.
quiz.placement: Teacher demonstration of the cheek smear: 'thin enough to read newsprint through it'

quiz.prompt: A learner has drawn a cheek cell and labelled the outer boundary as 'cell wall'. What is the correct response?
choices: The label is correct, because all cells have a cell wall
The outer boundary should be labelled 'nucleus'
The label is correct, because the stain makes the cell wall visible
The label is wrong: cheek cells have no cell wall, and the outer boundary is the cell membrane
quiz.rationale: Animal cells such as cheek cells lack a cell wall. Their outer boundary is a thin cell membrane, so a cell wall label is a misconception.
quiz.placement: Drawing Checklist Clipboard: checking that no cell wall is labelled on the cheek cell drawing

quiz.prompt: Cheek cells have no cell wall. What does this suggest about animal cells?
choices: They cannot have a nucleus
They are flexible and can have irregular shapes
They are always perfectly rectangular
They have no cell membrane
quiz.rationale: Without a rigid cell wall, animal cells can change or vary in shape. This helps explain how platelets can change form to help a clot form in a wound.
quiz.placement: Evidence Harvest T-chart and the 3-sentence explanation about the absence of a cell wall

quiz.prompt: When you update the plant half of your model, you write what a missing structure does in the plant cell. Which match between a structure and its function in a plant cell is correct?
choices: Cell wall: gives rigid support and a fixed shape
Large central vacuole: controls the cell's nucleus
Cell wall: lets the cell change shape easily
Chloroplast: makes the cell rigid
quiz.rationale: The cell wall is rigid and supports the plant cell, giving it a fixed shape. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, not support.
quiz.placement: Model update: writing one sentence for each structure ABSENT in the animal cell

lessons.title: Cell Specialisation: Meaning, Significance, and Specialised Animal Cells

quiz.prompt: In Biology, what does 'cell specialisation' mean, and why does it matter for a many-celled body such as a human?
choices: A cell changes its DNA each time it needs a new job
All cells in the body have the same shape so that each one can do every job
Only blood cells are specialised, so they do all the work of the body
A cell has a particular structure that suits it to one main job, so different cells can each do one job well and the body can do many things at once
quiz.rationale: Specialisation means a cell has a structure suited to one main job. Because different cells each do one job well, a many-celled body can clot blood, fight bacteria and rebuild skin at the same time.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher names the idea of cell specialisation after the sickle-cell discussion

quiz.prompt: A mature red blood cell has a biconcave shape and no nucleus. How does having no nucleus help the cell do its job?
choices: It lets the cell divide faster to make more red blood cells
It makes the cell long enough to carry signals
It lets the cell fight bacteria by engulfing them
It leaves more room for haemoglobin, so the cell can carry more oxygen
quiz.rationale: With no nucleus, there is more space inside the cell for haemoglobin, which carries oxygen to tissues such as healing skin.
quiz.placement: Observe: structured observation table, red blood cell, 'Features Absent' column

quiz.prompt: A red blood cell has no nucleus and lives for only about 120 days. Which statement best explains the link between these two facts?
choices: Without a nucleus the cell cannot repair itself or make new proteins, so it wears out after about 120 days
Without a nucleus the cell is too heavy to travel round the body for longer
Without a nucleus the cell is always attacked by white blood cells
Without a nucleus the cell uses up all its haemoglobin in 120 days
quiz.rationale: The missing nucleus gives more room for haemoglobin but has a cost: the cell cannot repair itself or make new proteins, so it has a short life.
quiz.placement: Observe: data card (red blood cell lives ~120 days, ~170,000 circuits)

quiz.prompt: A nerve cell (neuron) has a very long axon. How does this feature help the neuron do its job?
choices: It lets the cell contract and pull on bones
It allows a signal, such as pain from a fingertip, to travel a long distance to the brain
It gives the cell more space to store haemoglobin
It lets the cell swim towards other cells
quiz.rationale: A long axon lets one cell carry electrical signals over long distances, for example from a finger to the brain.
quiz.placement: Explain: Structure-Function Graphic Organiser, nerve cell row (long axon prompt)

quiz.prompt: A muscle cell (myocyte) contains many mitochondria. Why does this suit the cell's function?
choices: Mitochondria release the energy the cell needs for repeated contraction
Mitochondria carry oxygen around the body
Mitochondria make the cell long so it can carry signals
Mitochondria help the cell to engulf bacteria
quiz.rationale: Mitochondria release energy from respiration. A muscle cell contracts a lot, so it needs a large supply of energy.
quiz.placement: Explain: Structure-Function Graphic Organiser, muscle cell row (mitochondria prompt)

quiz.prompt: A sperm cell has a streamlined head, a long flagellum and a midpiece packed with mitochondria. What is the job of the midpiece?
choices: It supplies the energy the flagellum needs for swimming
It stores food for the early embryo
It carries oxygen to the head of the sperm
It protects the cell with a thick outer layer
quiz.rationale: The midpiece is packed with mitochondria, which release the energy needed to move the flagellum so the sperm can swim.
quiz.placement: Observe: evidence pack diagram of the sperm cell

quiz.prompt: Sickle-cell red blood cells still contain haemoglobin, yet a person with sickle-cell disease suffers from anaemia and blocked blood vessels. What is the best explanation?
choices: The curved, stiff cells cannot squeeze through the smallest vessels, so they block them, and they break down early so fewer red cells remain
The sickle cells have a very large nucleus that blocks the vessels
The sickle cells are too flexible and burst open in the blood vessels
The sickle cells have no haemoglobin at all, so they cannot carry oxygen
quiz.rationale: A changed gene makes the cells curved and stiff. They block narrow vessels, so tissues get less oxygen, and they break down early, so there are fewer red cells (anaemia). This shows that shape determines function.
quiz.placement: Explain: sickle-cell anaemia argument question (CER with micrograph comparison)

quiz.prompt: In the healing-cut activity, learners wrote 'not involved in healing' for the sperm cell. What does this show about specialisation?
choices: Sperm cells are not real cells because they play no part in healing
All specialised cells must help with wound healing
A cell is specialised for one main job, so not every cell takes part in every process
Specialised cells can change their structure to do any job needed
quiz.rationale: Each specialised cell has a structure suited to one main job. A sperm cell is built for reproduction, so it is not involved in healing a cut.
quiz.placement: Explain: 'Connection to the Healing Cut' column, sperm cell row

lessons.title: Specialised Plant Cells: Form Meets Function in the Bean Seedling

quiz.prompt: A root hair cell has a long, thin, tube-like extension that reaches between soil particles. How does this feature help the cell do its job?
choices: It carries sugars from the leaves down to the root
It holds many chloroplasts so the root can make food
It gives a large surface area so more water and mineral salts can be absorbed from the soil
It lets the cell open and close a pore to control water loss
quiz.rationale: The long root hair extension greatly increases the surface area in contact with soil water, so the cell absorbs water and mineral salts faster. Root hair cells have no chloroplasts and do not carry sugars.
quiz.placement: Observe: labelled drawing of the root hair cell (long tubular extension, large vacuole, thin cell wall)

quiz.prompt: A pair of guard cells is kidney-shaped, with a thick inner wall and a thin outer wall. When water enters the guard cells, what happens to the stoma and why?
choices: The stoma opens because the thin outer walls stretch more than the thick inner walls, so the cells bend apart
The stoma stays the same because guard cells have no control over water
The stoma opens because the guard cells lose their cytoplasm and become hollow
The stoma closes because the thick inner walls stretch more than the thin outer walls
quiz.rationale: When water enters, the thin outer walls stretch more than the thick inner walls, so the pair bends apart and opens the pore. When water leaves they straighten and the pore closes.
quiz.placement: Explain: Match-the-Card group activity, guard-cell CER (Claim-Evidence-Reasoning) presentation

quiz.prompt: Two photographs show stomata on leaves of the same kind of plant taken at the same time of day. In dry Turkana the stomata are mostly closed. In humid Kericho they are mostly open. Which explanation best fits the guard cells in Turkana?
choices: The guard cells lose water and become less swollen, so the pore closes and saves water
The guard cells have no chloroplasts, so they cannot open
The guard cells die and are replaced by xylem vessels
The guard cells gain extra water, swell, and close the pore
quiz.rationale: In dry conditions the plant is short of water. The guard cells lose water and become less swollen, so the pore closes and less water is lost.
quiz.placement: Observe: Turkana vs Kericho guard cell comparison (fingers 1 or 2)

quiz.prompt: A learner says: "A xylem vessel is still alive because it carries water up the plant." Which statement is correct?
choices: The xylem vessel is dead because it has end walls that block the flow of water
The xylem vessel is dead at maturity: it has no living contents, and the hollow lumen with strong lignified walls forms the pipe
The xylem vessel is alive but has no cell wall
The xylem vessel is alive and keeps a nucleus near its wall
quiz.rationale: Xylem vessels form from living cells that lose their contents. The hollow, lignified walls left behind form a pipe, so specialisation ends in the cell's death. They have no end walls.
quiz.placement: Explain: consolidation mini-lecture and exit-check sentence 'Is the xylem vessel alive?'

quiz.prompt: Phloem sieve tubes have perforated sieve plates at their ends. What is the function of these sieve plates?
choices: They let sugars flow from one sieve tube cell to the next
They make the walls strong with lignin so the tube does not collapse
They absorb water from the soil
They carry out photosynthesis in the stem
quiz.rationale: The holes in the sieve plates let dissolved sugars pass between neighbouring sieve tube cells. Lignin strengthening belongs to xylem, and photosynthesis and water absorption are done by other cells.
quiz.placement: Explain: consolidation mini-lecture point (c), sieve plates of phloem

quiz.prompt: Palisade mesophyll cells are tall and cylindrical and packed with many chloroplasts. How does this suit their function in the leaf?
choices: The many chloroplasts help the cells absorb water and mineral salts from the soil
The many chloroplasts make the cells hollow so water can pass through
The many chloroplasts let the cells open and close the stomata
The many chloroplasts trap a lot of light for photosynthesis
quiz.rationale: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll that traps light energy. Dense chloroplasts in palisade cells give a high rate of photosynthesis in the leaf.
quiz.placement: Explain: consolidation mini-lecture point (d), palisade cell chloroplast density and photosynthesis rate

quiz.prompt: A learner draws arrows to show how specialised cells work together in the root of a bean seedling. Which arrow correctly shows this?
choices: Guard cells absorb water from the soil, then phloem sieve tubes carry it to the root hairs
Palisade cells absorb mineral salts from the soil, then root hair cells carry them to the leaf
Xylem vessels absorb water from the soil, then root hair cells carry it up the stem
Root hair cells absorb water and mineral salts from the soil, then xylem vessels transport them upwards
quiz.rationale: Root hair cells absorb water and mineral salts, and xylem vessels carry them up the plant. The other options give the jobs to the wrong cells.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the 'Plant Side' to the Cell Specialisation Model, arrows for cells working together in the root

lessons.title: Cell Organisation: Cells → Tissues → Organs → Organ Systems → Organism

quiz.prompt: Under a microscope, many flat epidermal cells of the same type are packed tightly together in layers at the edge of a cut finger. What do we call this group of similar cells working together to do one job?
choices: An organ system
A single specialised cell
An organ
A tissue
quiz.rationale: Cells of the same type that group together to do one job form a tissue. Many epidermal cells together form epithelial tissue.
quiz.placement: Observe: ARES Evidence Card Set 10, Side A, cross-section of epithelial tissue (many epidermal cells)

quiz.prompt: In the school analogy, one Grade 10 student is like one cell, and a Grade 10 class of 42 students is like a tissue. Which biological level matches Mwangaza Secondary School as a whole, with all its classes, teachers and departments working together?
choices: An organ system
A cell
An organ
A tissue
quiz.rationale: A school is made of several different groups working together, like an organ made of different tissues. A class of similar students matches a tissue, not the whole school.
quiz.placement: Observe: Side B Kenyan school analogy and ARES Observation Table

quiz.prompt: Which cell in the healing cut finger is long and thin, has a large nucleus and plenty of rough endoplasmic reticulum, and makes collagen to rebuild the dermis?
choices: Epidermal cell
Fibroblast
Neutrophil
Platelet
quiz.rationale: The fibroblast is the elongated cell that makes and secretes collagen to rebuild the dermis. Platelets help clotting, neutrophils engulf bacteria, and epidermal cells close the surface.
quiz.placement: Observe: Healing Cells strip on Side A of Evidence Card Set 10

quiz.prompt: Why is the skin called an organ and not just a tissue?
choices: Because it is a group of organs, including hair, nails and sweat glands
Because it is made only of epidermal cells packed in layers
Because it is made of a very large number of cells
Because it is made of more than one tissue, such as epithelial tissue and connective tissue, working together
quiz.rationale: An organ is made of different tissues working together. The epidermis is epithelial tissue and the dermis (rebuilt by fibroblasts) is connective tissue, with blood vessels and nerves running through them.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher builds the five-level hierarchy diagram and discusses why skin is an organ

quiz.prompt: Which of these is an ORGAN SYSTEM?
choices: A fibroblast
The epidermis
The integumentary system (skin, hair, nails and sweat glands)
The skin
quiz.rationale: An organ system is a group of organs working together. The integumentary system combines the skin with hair, nails and sweat glands. The skin alone is one organ.
quiz.placement: Explain: hierarchy diagram and the prompt card on organ versus organ system

quiz.prompt: A Grade 10 student says: 'A single epidermal cell can heal a cut on a finger by itself.' Which response best corrects this claim?
choices: Each epidermal cell has different DNA, so they cannot work together
Only the whole organism can heal, and cells, tissues and organs play no part
Healing needs different cell types, such as platelets, neutrophils, fibroblasts and epidermal cells, working together within tissues, the skin and the body
Epidermal cells have no nucleus, so they cannot divide
quiz.rationale: No single cell does every job. Different specialised cells work inside tissues, tissues form the skin, and the systems of the organism work together to restore the finger. Epidermal cells do have an active nucleus and divide to close the wound.
quiz.placement: Explain: individual 5-sentence written explanation of why a single epidermal cell cannot heal a wound on its own

quiz.prompt: A learner is drawing Model Version 4 to show how an epidermal cell in a cut finger fits into the levels of organisation. Which nesting shows the correct order from smallest to largest?
choices: Epidermal cell → epithelial tissue → skin → integumentary system → human body
Epithelial tissue → epidermal cell → skin → human body → integumentary system
Epidermal cell → skin → epithelial tissue → integumentary system → human body
Epidermal cell → epithelial tissue → integumentary system → skin → human body
quiz.rationale: The order is cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism. So the epidermal cell forms epithelial tissue, which is part of the skin (organ), then the integumentary system, then the whole human body.
quiz.placement: Model: Version 4 hierarchy diagram nesting cells inside tissue, organ, organ system and organism

lessons.title: Synthesis and Model Revision: Putting the Cell Story Together

quiz.prompt: A student draws the organisation of the skin from the smallest level to the largest. Which order is correct?
choices: Skin organ, epidermal cell, epithelial tissue, whole organism, integumentary system
Epithelial tissue, epidermal cell, integumentary system, skin organ, whole organism
Epidermal cell, skin organ, epithelial tissue, whole organism, integumentary system
Epidermal cell, epithelial tissue, skin organ, integumentary system, whole organism
quiz.rationale: Cells join to form tissues, tissues form organs, organs work together in organ systems, and systems make up the whole organism. For skin this is epidermal cell, epithelial tissue, skin organ, integumentary system, organism.
quiz.placement: Zone D: Cell Organisation Hierarchy (cell to organism using the skin as the example)

quiz.prompt: Which structure is found in a plant cell but is absent from an animal cell?
choices: Cell wall
Cell membrane
Nucleus
Mitochondria
quiz.rationale: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall outside the cell membrane that supports the cell, and animal cells do not. Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, a nucleus and mitochondria.
quiz.placement: Zone A and Zone B: labelled plant cell and animal cell, noting two structures absent from the animal cell

quiz.prompt: Fibroblasts help to rebuild a wound by making and secreting collagen. Which structural feature of a fibroblast best matches this job?
choices: It is full of lysosomes, which digest the collagen
It has no nucleus, so it can be packed with collagen
It is flat and tightly packed, so it covers the wound surface
It is rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, which make and send out proteins
quiz.rationale: Collagen is a protein. Rough endoplasmic reticulum makes proteins and the Golgi apparatus processes and packages them for secretion, so fibroblasts are rich in both.
quiz.placement: Zone C: three specialised wound-healing cells with structure-function arrows (fibroblasts)

quiz.prompt: After a cut, neutrophils and macrophages move to the wound and engulf bacteria. Which feature helps them digest the bacteria once engulfed?
choices: They have many lysosomes containing digestive enzymes
They have no nucleus, so the bacteria cannot escape
They contain chloroplasts that make food from the bacteria
They have a cell wall that crushes the bacteria
quiz.rationale: Neutrophils and macrophages have an irregular shape and many lysosomes. Lysosomes contain enzymes that digest engulfed bacteria.
quiz.placement: Zone C: three specialised wound-healing cells with structure-function arrows (neutrophils or macrophages)

quiz.prompt: Which statement about platelets, the cell fragments that start clotting when you cut your finger, is correct?
choices: They are cells that make collagen to rebuild the skin
They are small cell fragments with no nucleus that become sticky when activated and start clotting
They are flat cells that divide and move across the wound to close the surface
They are large cells with a nucleus that engulf bacteria
quiz.rationale: Platelets are small cell fragments with no nucleus. When activated they become sticky and release clotting proteins to start clotting. The other descriptions fit neutrophils, fibroblasts and epidermal cells.
quiz.placement: Zone C: three specialised wound-healing cells (platelets)

quiz.prompt: Epidermal cells close the surface of a cut finger. Which description of these cells fits this job?
choices: Long cells rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum that make collagen
Flat, tightly packed cells that divide and migrate across the wound
Cells with many lysosomes that digest bacteria
Round cells with no nucleus that float in the blood
quiz.rationale: Epidermal cells are flat and tightly packed, and they divide and migrate to close the wound surface. This links their structure to their function of covering the wound.
quiz.placement: Zone C: three specialised wound-healing cells with structure-function arrows (epidermal cells)

quiz.prompt: Platelets, neutrophils, fibroblasts and epidermal cells all help to heal a cut, yet they look very different under a microscope. What is the best explanation?
choices: Each type of cell has a different shape and different organelles that suit its own job, so shape helps determine function
They are completely different organisms that happen to live in the skin
Only the cells with a nucleus have a specific job, so they all look different
Cell shape is random and has nothing to do with what the cell does
quiz.rationale: This answers the driving question. Cells are specialised, and each cell type has a shape and organelles suited to its job, such as clotting, engulfing bacteria, making collagen or covering the wound.
quiz.placement: DQB review: cumulative verbal answer to the driving question (why cells look so different and how shape determines the job a cell can do)

lessons.title: Consolidation, DQB Closure, and Final Explanation — The Healing Cut Fully Explained

quiz.prompt: When a finger is cut, platelets help to stop the bleeding. Which statement about platelets is correct?
choices: They are long cells that secrete collagen to rebuild the skin
They are tiny cell fragments with no nucleus that become sticky and release chemicals that start clotting
They are biconcave discs packed with haemoglobin that carry oxygen to the wound
They are large cells with a big nucleus that engulf bacteria
quiz.rationale: Platelets are small cell fragments without a nucleus. When activated they become sticky and release clotting chemicals that plug the cut. Engulfing bacteria, carrying oxygen and making collagen are jobs of other cells.
quiz.placement: Cold-call round, Stage 3 (clot forms): Student B on platelet structure

quiz.prompt: A clot is held together by a net of a protein called fibrin. Which cell structure makes proteins?
choices: Ribosomes
Cell membrane
Mitochondria
Lysosomes
quiz.rationale: Ribosomes, many of them on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, join amino acids to make proteins. Lysosomes digest materials and mitochondria release energy.
quiz.placement: Cold-call round, Stage 3 (clot continued): Student C on the organelle that makes proteins

quiz.prompt: Neutrophils arrive at a wound and engulf and digest bacteria. Which organelle, full of digestive enzymes, makes this digestion possible?
choices: Nucleus
Chloroplast
Cell wall
Lysosome
quiz.rationale: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down the bacteria the neutrophil has engulfed. Chloroplasts and cell walls are not found in animal cells, and the nucleus holds DNA rather than digesting material.
quiz.placement: Cold-call round, Stage 4 (immune response): Student D on neutrophils

quiz.prompt: Fibroblasts secrete collagen to rebuild tissue in a wound. Which organelle is highly developed in fibroblasts, and why?
choices: Lysosomes, because fibroblasts must digest bacteria before they can make collagen
Cell wall, because fibroblasts must stay stiff to close the wound
Rough endoplasmic reticulum, because collagen is a protein that the cell makes and sends out
Chloroplasts, because fibroblasts need to trap light energy to repair tissue
quiz.rationale: Collagen is a protein. Cells that make and secrete a lot of protein have much rough endoplasmic reticulum (with the Golgi apparatus). Fibroblasts are animal cells, so they have no chloroplasts or cell wall.
quiz.placement: Cold-call round, Stage 5 (tissue rebuilding): Student F on fibroblasts

quiz.prompt: Epidermal cells divide to close the surface of a wound. What must happen inside an epidermal cell before it can divide?
choices: The cell must lose its nucleus, as red blood cells do
The cell wall must grow thicker to separate the new cells
The nucleus must copy the cell's DNA, and mitochondria must supply the energy
The lysosomes must release collagen into the cell
quiz.rationale: Before division the nucleus copies its DNA so each new cell gets a full set, and mitochondria supply the energy. Epidermal cells keep their nucleus and, as animal cells, have no cell wall.
quiz.placement: Cold-call round, Stage 6 (skin closes): Student G on epidermal cells

quiz.prompt: Most cells in one person's body that have a nucleus carry the same DNA. Why do skin cells and white blood cells look so different?
choices: White blood cells have no DNA, so they cannot look like skin cells
Skin cells use all their genes, while white blood cells use none
They have different DNA, because each cell type inherited its DNA from a different parent cell
Each cell type has different genes switched on, so it makes the structures and proteins its job needs
quiz.rationale: Specialisation happens because different genes are switched on in different cells, so each cell makes the structures and proteins needed for its own job. The DNA itself is the same in all cells that have a nucleus.
quiz.placement: Cold-call round, Synthesis: Student H on why cells with the same DNA look so different

quiz.prompt: Which of these structures is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
choices: Mitochondria
Cell membrane
Nucleus
Cell wall
quiz.rationale: Plant cells have a cell wall (and chloroplasts and a large vacuole). Animal cells do not have a cell wall. The cell membrane, nucleus and mitochondria are found in both.
quiz.placement: 'Then vs. Now' written comparison, using the word wall (organelle, cell wall, chloroplast, vacuole, etc.)

quiz.prompt: During Driving Question Board closure, a question card asks something that needs more biology than the class has learned in this sub-strand. How should the class classify it?
choices: ANSWERED
It should be removed from the board
PARTIALLY ANSWERED
BEYOND THIS UNIT
quiz.rationale: A question that needs more biology than has been learned so far is classed as BEYOND THIS UNIT and moved to the Future Questions Wall. ANSWERED means there is strong evidence, and PARTIALLY ANSWERED means some evidence but gaps remain.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board closure: classifying cards as ANSWERED, PARTIALLY ANSWERED or BEYOND THIS UNIT
